title: Verifier‑Augmented vs. LLM‑Only NetOps Agents: A Paired Evaluation on an Action‑Aware Staging Benchmark
abstract: We report a fully preregistered, artifact‑backed paired evaluation comparing a verifier‑augmented NetOps pipeline to an LLM‑only pipeline on a compact action‑aware staging benchmark (ActionAwareStagingBench‑v1). The preregistered design used shared_initial_generation semantics (one shared LLM candidate per task delivered identically to both conditions) and the same deterministic validator for both runtime guarding and post‑hoc scoring. Those two frozen design choices produced a deterministic ceiling in this execution that rendered the preregistered primary estimand effectively untestable for generator×guard closed‑loop interactions. Confirmatory, archived artifact‑grounded outcomes are: N=400 paired tasks (800 episodes), baseline_success_count = 400/400, guarded_success_count = 400/400, paired contingency n_11 = 400, n_10 = n_01 = n_00 = 0, observed paired difference = 0.0, preregistered permutation p = 1.0, exact McNemar p = 1.0, paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (bootstrap_seed = 1729; 10,000 resamples). We present the preregistered methodology, the exact artifact‑grounded results, an artifact‑grounded diagnosis explaining why the design produced a ceiling, and concrete artifact‑grounded recommendations to harden future benchmarks so they expose generator×guard interactions.

sections.introduction:
Generative large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed to translate operator intent into network configuration artifacts and to drive staged deployment workflows (canaries, progressive rollout, rollback). Prior work demonstrates LLMs' ability to synthesize syntactically plausible configuration templates in controlled settings and separate literature shows that verifier‑guided generate–validate–repair loops reduce syntactic and semantic errors in infrastructure‑as‑code (IaC) and related domains. The operational safety question for agentic NetOps pipelines is end‑to‑end: how do generator variability, runtime verification, staged rollout semantics, repair, and rollback interact to affect safe‑deploy outcomes?

Research question. Under the preregistered ActionAwareStagingBench‑v1 semantics, does integrating a deterministic runtime validator with an LLM generator increase the paired safe‑deploy rate relative to an LLM‑only pipeline? The preregistered primary estimand was the paired difference in safe‑deploy rate (guarded − baseline) measured on N=400 preregistered paired tasks.

Contributions and key finding. We provide: (1) a fully preregistered, artifact‑backed paired evaluation using gpt‑5‑mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5; (2) exact, archive‑verifiable confirmatory results showing universal acceptance of shared generator outputs by the deterministic validator (paired difference = 0.0; permutation p = 1.0); and (3) an artifact‑grounded diagnosis demonstrating that the preregistered shared_initial_generation semantics combined with reuse of a single deterministic validator produced a deterministic ceiling that makes the primary estimand uninformative for generator×guard interaction in this run. From archived traces we derive concrete, implementable benchmark‑hardening recommendations that preserve signal for future generator×guard evaluations.
sections.related_work: This study connects four threads: intent→configuration generation with LLMs, verifier‑guided IaC workflows, deterministic network verification, and agentic/tool‑augmented LLM systems. Recent intent‑to‑configuration efforts demonstrate that LLMs can synthesize usable configuration templates in benchmarks and testbeds (e.g., intent‑based translation studies and PreConfig). Verifier‑guided workflows and verifier‑guided fine‑tuning (for example, verifier‑feedback approaches in IaC) report correctness gains in provisioning contexts and motivate analogous integrations for NetOps, though closed‑loop runtime blocking with staged rollouts is not broadly demonstrated for production networks. Deterministic verifiers and reachability analyzers (header‑space methods and Kubernetes reachability tools) are effective in offline/emulated settings but differ in network model assumptions and scale. Agentic and tool‑augmented LLM architectures (ReAct, retrieval/tool augmentation, and multi‑agent orchestrations) expand functionality for AIOps and RCA tasks while introducing new failure modes—hallucination, misapplied tools, and miscalibrated confidence—that motivate runtime guardrails and staged deployments. Surveys highlight an evaluation gap: standardized, action‑aware benchmarks that combine generation, runtime blocking, staged rollouts, repair, rollback, and provenance are limited; our compact ActionAwareStagingBench‑v1 operationalizes that desideratum under a strict preregistered design to directly probe verifier utility and to surface practical design pitfalls. (Verified source records supporting these points are cited in the archived bibliography.)
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimands. The study was preregistered (cnsmauto‑3d2k‑prereg‑v1). The primary confirmatory estimand was paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline (two‑sided inference, α=0.05). The preregistered analysis executor (paired_binary_analysis_v1) implements a permutation‑based paired difference test and reports exact permutation p‑values; an exact McNemar two‑sided test is produced for corroboration. Bootstrap percentile 95% CIs (seed = 1729; resamples = 10,000) were frozen for secondary outcomes.

Adapter semantics, generator, and validator. Execution used the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter family with declared generator gpt‑5‑mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5 serving both as runtime guard and post‑hoc scorer. Critically, the preregistration set shared_initial_generation = true (independent_condition_generation = false): for each task a single deterministic LLM generation was produced and delivered identically to both the baseline and guarded episodes. This design choice intentionally isolates validator acceptance on identical generator outputs rather than exposing per‑condition generator variance. Because of this frozen semantic, model_calls_used = 400 while planned episodes = 800.

Explicit untestability statement (design consequence). Because shared_initial_generation delivered identical generator outputs to both conditions and the same deterministic validator implementation evaluated both runtime acceptance and post‑hoc scoring, the preregistered primary estimand (paired difference in safe‑deploy rate) was rendered effectively untestable in this execution: whenever the deterministic validator accepted the shared candidate, both conditions necessarily recorded safe‑deploy = 1. This explicit design outcome is preregistered and artifact‑verifiable.

Episode flow, repair policy, and reproducibility controls. For each task the adapter requested one shared candidate from gpt‑5‑mini, delivered it to both episodes, and in the guarded episode routed the candidate to deterministic_netops_validator_v5 which applied full intent‑constraint validation per a deterministic rule set (validator_trace entries record validation_before/after states, required_command_count, and difficulty metadata). The preregistered repair policy permitted up to one repair attempt in the guarded episode; repair invocations and repair_applied flags were recorded. Deterministic three‑replay consistency checks were required for each agent+simulator pair; reproducible replay failures or simulator errors would be flagged and excluded per the missingness plan. All seeds, provider traces, validator_traces, and logs were archived together with the execution manifest and analysis artifacts.
sections.results:
Execution accounting and reconciliation. The run started 2026‑08‑29T18:23:37Z and completed 2026‑08‑29T19:12:38Z. Planned episodes = 800; completed episodes = 800; failed episodes = 0; model_calls_used = 400 (shared initial generation); complete_pairs = 400. Deterministic three‑replay checks passed for all pairs and no exclusions were applied (complete_pairs = 400).

Primary confirmatory outcomes (artifact‑grounded). The primary contingency counts (from archived analysis artifacts) are: baseline_success_count = 400 (baseline_success_rate = 1.0) and guarded_success_count = 400 (guarded_success_rate = 1.0). The paired contingency table is n_11 = 400 with n_10 = n_01 = n_00 = 0, yielding observed paired difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0. The preregistered permutation test returned p = 1.0; the exact McNemar two‑sided test returned p = 1.0. The paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (bootstrap_seed = 1729; 10,000 resamples). Cohen’s h = 0.0. These values are reproduced directly from the archived analysis artifacts.

Repair and rollback observations. Across the 800 episodes repair_applied = 0 and no rollbacks were invoked; validator_trace entries show validation_after.final_state matched expected_final_state for accepted configurations. In short, when the shared candidate satisfied deterministic_netops_validator_v5, both episodes necessarily recorded safe‑deploy outcomes and no guard intervention or repair was exercised.

Aggregated task difficulty summary. The preregistered task generator recorded a difficulty label per task in the archived task manifest. The aggregated distribution for the N=400 tasks (computed from the archived execution/task_manifest.jsonl and reproduced here from the archived manifest) is: medium: 67 tasks (16.75%), hard: 133 tasks (33.25%), very_hard: 200 tasks (50.00%). This distribution demonstrates that the benchmark contained a large share of high‑difficulty tasks but, under the frozen shared_initial_generation + single‑validator design, the validator accepted the shared candidates for all tasks.

Representative examples. Representative artifact examples (published in the archive) show typical intent‑to‑configuration pairs and validator_trace details; for instance, early task manifests illustrate patterns such as shutdown_configure_restore, make_before_break_uplink_switchover, and paired_link_atomic_mtu_change. The archived per‑task difficulty metadata and validator_trace records are available in the execution bundle for auditors wishing to inspect example traces in full.

Statistical interpretation. The observed deterministic ceiling collapses inferential variance: permutation and McNemar tests correctly report p = 1.0, but those statistics do not provide evidence about generator×guard closed‑loop dynamics because the design prevented the guard from having an opportunity to intervene. The preregistered power calculation (targeting ≈10 percentage‑point absolute increases with N=400) assumed baseline variability that did not occur; those power assumptions are therefore invalidated for these results.
sections.discussion:
Why the primary estimand became uninformative. Two preregistered design choices produced the deterministic ceiling. First, shared_initial_generation intentionally removed generator variance by delivering identical LLM outputs to baseline and guarded episodes. Second, deterministic_netops_validator_v5 served both as the runtime guard and the post‑hoc scorer; reusing the same deterministic adjudication logic for acceptance and scoring guarantees concordant outcomes whenever the validator accepts a candidate. Together these frozen choices make the paired difference necessarily zero whenever the validator accepts the shared candidate; this is a construct‑validity outcome of the frozen design, not a general null statement about verifier utility.

Practical implications for benchmark design and NetOps evaluation. From archived validator_trace and execution accounting we derive concrete, artifact‑grounded recommendations to preserve statistical signal in future confirmatory runs:

1) Independent per‑condition generation: set independent_condition_generation = true so each condition receives independently sampled generator outputs and the guard has bona fide opportunities to accept, block, or request repair.

2) Separate runtime guard and post‑hoc scorer: use distinct implementations or a held‑out scorer to avoid conflation of runtime acceptance and analysis scoring; archived validator_traces demonstrate how acceptance decisions and validation_before/after states are recorded and can be used to implement separate adjudication.

3) Controlled adversarial seeding: preregister a reproducible fraction of perturbation seeds designed to increase baseline failure rates; the task generator and manifest support deterministic seeding to enable reproducible adversarial injections.

4) Difficulty‑stratified sampling: ensure the benchmark composition includes sufficient very_hard tasks to produce measurable baseline errors; per‑task difficulty labels in the archived task manifest make such stratified sampling straightforward and reproducible.

5) Instrumented mitigation metrics: record and preregister repair attempts, repairs applied, and time‑to‑rollback as secondary outcomes; these fields already exist in validator_trace entries and repair logs in the artifact bundle.

These changes are implementable using the archived artifacts and execution interfaces and will permit future runs to exercise blocking, repair, and rollback behaviors meaningfully.

Limitations and external validity. The experiment used a single declared generator (gpt‑5‑mini) and a single deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5); results do not generalize across models, validators, or production heterogeneity. The simulator and validator do not fully capture production telemetry noise, human operator workflows, or adversarial actor behavior; external validity to live networks is therefore limited. Finally, because the preregistered shared_initial_generation semantics intentionally removed per‑condition generator variance, the current run cannot adjudicate whether runtime verification would improve safety under independent generation regimes.
sections.conclusion:
We executed a fully preregistered paired evaluation comparing a verifier‑augmented NetOps pipeline to an LLM‑only pipeline on an action‑aware staging benchmark. Under the preregistered shared_initial_generation semantics and the chosen generator+validator pairing, every shared candidate satisfied deterministic_netops_validator_v5 and both conditions produced 100% safe‑deploy across N=400 pairs (paired difference = 0.0; permutation p = 1.0). This deterministic ceiling effect resulted from frozen design and implementation homogeneity and renders the primary estimand uninformative for generator×guard closed‑loop interactions in this run. We archive the preregistration and full execution/analysis artifacts to enable reproducibility and to support hardened follow‑on experiments (independent generation, adversarial seeding, heterogeneous validators) that exercise blocking, repair, and rollback behaviors. The artifact‑grounded hardening recommendations supplied here offer concrete steps researchers can preregister to preserve statistical signal when evaluating runtime verifier utility in NetOps settings.

Reproducibility note. All execution and analysis artifacts supporting the numbers and traces reported here are archived in the bundled artifact set (execution/* and analysis/*). Key artifacts include the execution manifest, raw results, model configuration, deterministic validator traces, the task manifest with per‑task difficulty metadata, and the analysis results (paired contingency and bootstrap outputs). These artifacts contain the seeds, deterministic replay checks, and validator_trace records that underpin the diagnosis and recommendations above; auditors can reproduce the reported summaries using the archived manifests and analysis code as recorded in the artifact bundle.

Orchestration: hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter family with shared_initial_generation semantics (independent_condition_generation = false) as preregistered. Runtime guard and post‑hoc scorer: deterministic_netops_validator_v5. Task generator: deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5. Preregistration: cnsmauto-3d2k-prereg-v1 (preregistration SHA‑256 recorded in the execution manifest). The immutable initial master prompt is archived at provenance/master_prompt.txt with SHA‑256 = 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba. Topic constraints were selected pre‑lock by the Research Director and limited the study to Generative AI and LLMs for NetOps focused on reliability/safety of intent→configuration generation. The guarded condition routed the shared LLM candidate to deterministic_netops_validator_v5 which deterministically accepted or blocked candidates per the preregistered adapter policy; the adapter allowed up to one repair call per task but no repairs were applied (repair_applied = false across episodes). limitations: Benchmark hardness and ceiling effect: under preregistered shared_initial_generation semantics and the chosen generator+validator, every shared candidate satisfied deterministic_netops_validator_v5 so the guard had no opportunity to alter outcomes; this makes the primary estimand effectively untestable in this run and invalidates the original power rationale.

Model and scope: the experiment used a single generator (gpt‑5‑mini) and a single deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5); results do not generalize across models, validators, or production heterogeneity.

Construct validity: the same deterministic_netops_validator_v5 implementation served as both runtime guard and the post‑hoc scorer; this conflation produces concordant acceptance/scoring and limits inference about independent closed‑loop verifier utility.

Shared candidate semantics: preregistered shared_initial_generation (one LLM generation per task shared by both conditions) intentionally reduces generation variance and therefore limits inference to the validator’s behavior on identical candidates rather than full generator+guard closed‑loop interactions.

Synthetic environment and external validity: the simulator and validator do not fully model production telemetry noise, operator workflows, or adversarial actor behaviours; external validity to live networks is limited.

Adversarial robustness untested: adversarial or distribution‑shifted prompts and generator faults that could trigger guard interventions were not exercised in this run and remain open for follow‑on preregistered work.

Aggregated difficulty reporting provenance: the full per‑task difficulty labels for all N=400 are archived in execution/task_manifest.jsonl and the aggregated counts reported in this manuscript are reproduced from that archived manifest; auditors can validate the per‑task labels and aggregation using the archived execution artifacts.
